subject: AI & Agents
title: Why AI Hallucinates
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Why AI Hallucinates.

hook.text: Ask an AI for a source and it might cite a paper that doesn't exist — confidently.

buildup.text: Language models generate the most probable next words. Probability isn't truth.

discovery.text: When the model lacks knowledge, it fills the gap with plausible-sounding fiction.

twist.text: A lawyer submitted AI-generated legal briefs citing six fake court cases. The judge wasn't amused.

climax.text: Hallucination is a feature of how generation works, not a bug that can be simply patched.

quiz.question: Why do language models 'hallucinate'?
options: They generate probable text, not verified truth

details.summary: AI hallucinations occur because language models predict statistically likely text, not verified facts. Confident fabrication is an inherent feature of the prediction process, not a bug that can be simply patched.
details.whyItMatters: Hallucinations make AI unreliable for factual research, medical advice, and legal references. Understanding the root cause helps users apply appropriate skepticism and verification practices.
takeaways: Hallucinations arise from statistical prediction, not fact retrieval
The model has no mechanism for verifying truth or accuracy
Reducing hallucinations is possible but eliminating them currently is not

faq.question: Can hallucinations be completely eliminated?
faq.answer: Unlikely with current architectures. Retrieval-augmented generation and fact-checking layers reduce frequency. But as long as models generate based on probability rather than verified knowledge, some hallucinations will occur.

faq.question: How can users protect themselves from AI hallucinations?
faq.answer: Always verify important AI claims against authoritative sources. Be especially cautious with citations, statistics, and specific facts. Use AI for drafting and exploration, not as a sole source of truth.
